summary:
The bill, titled the “Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024,” makes changes across several areas of tax law. Its primary purpose is to modify the child tax credit for working families, revive certain business tax incentives, establish a special tax framework for qualifying residents of Taiwan, provide tax relief for specific disaster victims, and adjust low-income housing credit rules.

For the child tax credit, the bill changes how the refundable portion is calculated for tax years 2023 through 2025. It introduces a per-child calculation and increases the maximum refundable amount each year, reaching $2,000 for 2025. Beginning with tax year 2024, the $2,000 credit amount is indexed for inflation. It also allows taxpayers to use their prior year’s earned income to calculate the credit, starting after 2023, and instructs the Treasury to automatically redetermine credits for early filers in the 2023 tax year who would benefit from these changes.

For businesses, the bill delays the requirement to amortize domestic research and experimental expenditures, allowing immediate expensing for costs paid or incurred in tax years beginning before 2026. It extends the allowance for depreciation, amortization, or depletion when calculating the business interest deduction limitation, generally applying to tax years after 2023, with an option for retroactive application. It extends 100% bonus depreciation through 2026 and raises the maximum amount a business can expense for depreciable assets under Section 179, with these increased limits indexed for inflation starting in 2024.

Regarding Taiwan, the bill adds a new tax code section providing reduced withholding rates and other special rules for income from U.S. sources received by qualified residents of Taiwan, conditioned on Taiwan providing reciprocal benefits to U.S. persons. A separate subtitle authorizes the President to negotiate and enter into a broader tax agreement with Taiwan, subject to congressional approval and implementing legislation.

For disaster relief, the bill extends the rules for certain disaster-related personal casualty losses. It excludes from gross income qualified wildfire relief payments received between 2020 and 2025 for losses from federally declared wildfire disasters occurring after 2014. It also treats payments related to the February 2023 East Palestine train derailment as qualified disaster relief payments, effective for amounts received on or after the derailment date.

For housing, the bill increases the low-income housing tax credit ceiling for 2023 through 2025 and modifies the tax-exempt bond financing requirement to allow a lower percentage threshold for buildings financed by certain bonds issued before 2026.

The bill raises the threshold for information reporting on certain payments from $600 to $1,000, adjusted for inflation after 2024, and includes anti-fraud measures targeting COVID-related employee retention credits (ERTC). These include increased penalties for promoters, new due diligence requirements, an extension of the assessment limitation period to six years, and a January 31, 2024, filing deadline for claiming credits or refunds for the ERTC.
